persona_label: Wu Guiying — Multi-morbid older woman, long-term smoker, overwhelmed and scattered, with a distributed lung-cancer red flag each fragment of which she has attributed to an existing condition
target_ground_truth: A 71F, ~40-pack-year smoker with COPD, presenting as an overwhelmed multi-morbid patient (type 2 diabetes with erratic sugars, AF on anticoagulation, ischaemic heart disease / stable angina, hypertension, CKD ~stage 3, osteoarthritis, low mood, polypharmacy across four uncoordinated services) asking for help rationalising her tablets and her sugars. The decisive finding is a DISTRIBUTED red flag: no single alarming statement, but an assembly of fragments each pre-attributed to an existing condition — (1) a chronic smoker's/COPD cough that has CHANGED over ~2 months (more frequent, different, more productive), buried under 'same as always' (the hinge fact); (2) new small-volume haemoptysis (blood flecks a handful of times over recent weeks), written off to 'coughing hard' and to her blood thinner; (3) unintentional weight loss ~6 kg over ~3 months, recast as 'one good thing' and blamed on her diabetes; (4) reduced appetite, blamed on low mood / cooking for one; (5) marked fatigue, blamed on everything and therefore nothing; (6) a softer new right shoulder/upper-back ache, blamed on arthritis. Assembled — a heavy smoker with a changed chronic cough, new haemoptysis, unintentional weight loss and anorexia — this is a suspected LUNG CANCER until proven otherwise. The anticoagulant is a TRAP, not an explanation: haemoptysis on a blood thinner still requires investigation. Each element is individually explained by a comorbidity (diagnostic overshadowing); only the integration is alarming, so this tests INTEGRATION across multi-morbidity, not detection of a single symptom. Correct handling: resist getting absorbed in the med-reconciliation and sugars (her manageable ask), listen holistically, and pull the threads together (has the cough changed and when; when did the weight loss start and was it intentional; tell me about the blood) to assemble the cluster; identify it as a possible lung cancer needing URGENT assessment — urgent chest X-ray and an urgent suspected-cancer referral, days-not-weeks — calmly, without blunt cancer-naming up front and WITHOUT 999 for small-volume haemoptysis with no acute features; counter the attributions (a changed smoker's cough is not 'the usual'; weight loss is not a silver lining; blood is not the anticoagulant); safety-net for large-volume haemoptysis or breathlessness at rest; and acknowledge/triage her genuine other needs (the medication muddle, the sugars) so her whole-picture plea is heard without displacing the priority — all in a manageable, one-or-two-priorities, non-catastrophising register for an exhausted, defeated woman. The dominant, easiest-to-commit failure is the under-call: helping with the tablets and sugars, treating the chest as stable COPD, and — because she takes reassurance literally — actively closing a lung cancer.
levels_note: Closest to target first; each level includes everything below it. The red flag is distributed, so the core competence is integration across fragments, not detecting one symptom. Disposition is urgent suspected-cancer referral (days-not-weeks), not emergency and not routine. Most dangerous and easiest failure is the under-call (overshadowing collusion), listed first under L0.

levels.label: Complete picture
levels.credit_when: Transcript shows everything in L3, AND: (1) corrects the two load-bearing beliefs specifically — a CHANGED smoker's cough is not 'the usual', and unintentional weight loss is not a silver lining — and gently dismantles the 'you can't chase everything / my specialists would have caught anything serious' resignation for THIS cluster, naming the fragmented-care gap kindly (exactly what gets missed when four teams each see one part); (2) acknowledges and briefly triages her genuine other problems — offering to help with the medication muddle and the erratic sugars so her whole-picture plea is heard — without letting them displace the priority; (3) delivers all of it in a manageable, one-or-two-priorities way calibrated to an exhausted, defeated woman (not a long checklist), warm and non-catastrophising, surfacing the protective avoidance gently (she had half-noticed and been frightened) so she engages rather than shuts down or turns fatalistic.

levels.label: Gets the mechanism
levels.credit_when: Transcript shows everything in L2, AND the coach identifies the assembled cluster as a possible LUNG CANCER (red flag until proven otherwise given the ~40-pack-year history) requiring URGENT assessment — urgent chest X-ray and an urgent suspected-cancer referral, on a days-not-weeks timeframe — calibrated correctly: NOT emergency 999 for small-volume haemoptysis with no acute features, and NOT routine. Delivers it calmly, framing it as a specific pattern needing a prompt proper look rather than bluntly declaring cancer in a way that frightens her, and provides safety-netting for large-volume haemoptysis or breathlessness at rest. Has not yet corrected the load-bearing beliefs or acknowledged her other genuine needs.

levels.label: Questions the surface
levels.credit_when: Transcript shows everything in L1, AND the coach INTEGRATES across her scattered account rather than answering fragment-by-fragment — pulling the threads together with the linking questions (has the cough changed and when; when did the weight loss start and was it intentional; tell me about the blood) — and establishes the hinge (the chronic cough has CHANGED over ~2 months) alongside the unintentional weight loss, anorexia, and new haemoptysis in a heavy smoker. Explicitly counters the attributions, including the anticoagulant trap (haemoptysis on a blood thinner still needs investigating, not explaining away). Recognises this as one coherent cluster, not six separate comorbidity flare-ups. Has not yet named/calibrated the disposition or done the belief/relational work.

levels.label: Right zone, wrong depth
levels.credit_when: Transcript shows the coach senses the chest/cough thread matters and does not simply do the med-sorting-and-sugars task she asked for — it flags the cough/weight as worth a proper look and steers toward getting the chest checked, staying calm and not burying her in a checklist. BUT it does not integrate the fragments into a single cluster, establish that the cough CHANGED, or counter the attributions, so the significance and urgency aren't established. Right instinct (not fully absorbed in the manageable task, elevates the chest), but the pattern isn't assembled.

levels.label: Wrong picture
levels.credit_when: Coach reaches the wrong handling. Tag one of the sub-modes below.

tags.label: under-action / overshadowing collusion
tags.credit_when: Coach accepts the attributions, helps with the medications and the sugars, and treats the chest as stable COPD — colluding with the diagnostic overshadowing, missing a possible lung cancer, and (because she takes reassurance literally) actively closing the issue. The most dangerous failure in the set, and the easiest to commit while looking maximally helpful.

tags.label: over-action / miscalibrated alarm
tags.credit_when: Coach bluntly declares probable cancer, OR directs her to emergency services now, for small-volume haemoptysis with no acute features — wrong tempo (this is urgent-referral, not 999) — and/or fires a rapid-fire checklist at an already-overwhelmed woman, tipping an exhausted, fatalistic person into shutdown or 'what's the point'.
